content: Routine infant immunization with the 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV7) since 2000 has significantly reduced the incidence of invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) in young children. However, cases of IPD caused by non-PCV7 serotypes, particularly serotype 19A, have increased. IPD is defined as the isolation of Streptococcus pneumoniae from a normally sterile body site, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid, in individuals residing in surveillance areas. These areas include Connecticut, Minnesota, New Mexico, and selected counties in California, Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, New York, Oregon, and Tennessee. IPD remains a leading cause of severe illness in children and adults worldwide. Following the introduction of PCV7, IPD rates among children under 5 years of age in the United States decreased by 76%. However, the rise in IPD cases caused by non-PCV7 serotypes, especially 19A, has partially offset these reductions. In February 2010, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommended the use of a newly licensed 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13). PCV13 includes the seven serotypes in PCV7 (4, 6B, 9V, 14, 18C, 19F, and 23F) and six additional serotypes (1, 3, 5, 6A, 7F, and 19A). To assess the vaccine-preventable burden of IPD among children under 5 years of age in the United States, the CDC and investigators analyzed 2007 data from the Active Bacterial Core surveillance (ABCs) system. Among 427 IPD cases with known serotypes in children under 5 years, 64% (274 cases) were caused by serotypes included in PCV13. Of these, 95% (260 cases) were due to three of the six additional serotypes in PCV13 (3, 7F, and 19A), with serotype 19A accounting for 42% of all cases. In 2007, an estimated 4,600 IPD cases occurred in children under 5 years in the United States, including approximately 2,900 cases caused by serotypes covered by PCV13, compared to only 70 cases caused by PCV7 serotypes. The use of PCV13 has the potential to further reduce IPD in the United States. Post-licensure monitoring will be essential to evaluate the vaccine's effectiveness in different populations and to track changes in disease burden caused by non-PCV13 serotypes. The ABCs system, part of the Emerging Infections Program Network, conducts populationand laboratory-based active surveillance. During 2006–2007, IPD surveillance was conducted in multiple states, covering a population of approximately 1 million children under 5 years. In 2007, 493 children under 5 years with IPD were identified in the ABCs population, with serotype information available for 87% (427 cases). Among these, children under 12 months accounted for 36% of cases, and those aged 12–23 months accounted for 29%. The overall rate of IPD was 22 cases per 100,000 population. Among children aged 24–59 months, IPD rates decreased with increasing age. The proportion of IPD cases caused by PCV13 serotypes was similar across age groups, ranging from 59% to 71%. The proportions were also comparable across racial groups, with 61% in Black children, 62% in children of other races, and 67% in White children. Hospitalization and clinical outcome data were available for 99% of serotyped IPD cases. Among 272 children with IPD caused by PCV13 serotypes, 62% were hospitalized, and 2% died. Clinical presentations included bacteremia without a confirmed source (37%), meningitis (9%), and pneumonia with bacteremia (42%). Based on the 2007 IPD rate of 22 cases per 100,000 children under 5 years, an estimated 4,600 cases occurred in this age group in the United States. Of these, 70 cases were caused by PCV7 serotypes, and 2,900 cases were caused by PCV13 serotypes. During 2006–2007, 301 IPD cases with known serotypes occurred among children aged 24–59 months, with 10% of cases occurring in high-risk children recommended for vaccination with the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23). Among these high-risk cases, 42% were caused by PCV13 serotypes, 13% by serotypes included in PPSV23 but not PCV13, and 45% by serotypes not covered by either vaccine. The introduction of PCV7 led to substantial reductions in IPD caused by vaccine serotypes among both vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, demonstrating indirect (herd) effects. This was attributed to reduced nasopharyngeal carriage of pneumococcus in vaccinated children and decreased transmission to unvaccinated individuals. Immunization with PCV13 is also expected to have herd effects among adults. However, the potential herd effects of PCV13 on serotypes 1 and 5, which are rarely found in the nasopharynx, remain uncertain. These serotypes are relatively uncommon causes of IPD in the United States. Although pneumonia hospitalization rates decreased after PCV7 introduction among children under 2 years, the effects of PCV13 on noninvasive diseases, such as nonbacteremic pneumonia and otitis media, are difficult to evaluate due to the lack of standardized case definitions, sensitive diagnostic methods, and routine surveillance for these conditions. Post-licensure monitoring of PCV13 is crucial to characterize its impact on disease burden and serotype distribution. On February 24, 2010, PCV13 was licensed by the FDA for the prevention of IPD caused by the 13 pneumococcal serotypes covered by the vaccine and for the prevention of otitis media caused by serotypes in the PCV7 formulation. PCV13 is approved for use in children aged 6 weeks to 71 months and replaces PCV7. The ACIP recommends routine vaccination with PCV13 for all children aged 2–59 months and for children aged 60–71 months with underlying medical conditions that increase their risk for pneumococcal disease or complications.
